kurz: Since the base interest rate has been back above 3%, distributing and accumulating ETFs are taxed the same in most years; differences arise in weak years, on reinvestment and in the withdrawal phase.

bloecke.md:
A distributing and an accumulating ETF on the same index hold the same shares. Often they are even two share classes of the same fund with the same portfolio, the same management and the same total expense ratio, differing only in their ISIN. For the Vanguard FTSE All-World, IE00BK5BQT80 stands for the accumulating class and IE00B3RBWM25 for the class that distributes quarterly, both with a TER of 0.14%. For the Kommer ETF, they are IE0001UQQ933 and IE000FPWSL69. The choice between the two classes therefore changes nothing about the investment itself. It determines when money leaves the fund assets and when taxes become due.

On the distribution date, money flows from the fund to the settlement account, and the unit price falls by the same amount. An investor with 100 units at €120 who receives €1.50 per unit then has €150 in cash and 100 units at €118.50, so their wealth is unchanged. The accumulating fund reinvests the same amount internally, and its unit price remains correspondingly higher. Differences in portfolio value after twenty years therefore arise only from taxes and from costs and delays in reinvestment.
A distribution does not increase wealth. It moves money from the fund to the account and in the process turns unrealised growth in value into taxable income.

## Base return and advance lump sum

Germany also taxes accumulating funds on an ongoing basis. Until 2017, this was done via deemed distributed income (ausschüttungsgleiche Erträge), that is, the interest and dividends retained in the fund, and since the 2018 investment tax reform it has been done via a flat-rate amount. The basis of this flat-rate amount is the base return (Basisertrag) under Section 18 InvStG (Investment Tax Act). It is calculated as the redemption price on the first valuation day of the year times the base interest rate (Basiszins) times 0.7, with the factor 0.7 representing a flat-rate cost deduction. The Bundesbank derives the base interest rate from the yield curve for federal securities with a remaining maturity of fifteen years, and the Federal Ministry of Finance publishes it. For 2026 it is 3.20% (BMF circular of 13 January 2026). This is the highest value since the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale) was introduced. The base return is therefore 2.24% of the value at the start of the year.

For comparing the two variants, a single clause in the law is decisive. Under it, the year's distributions are deducted from the base return. The [[Advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)|advance lump sum]] is therefore not an additional burden for accumulating funds. For a distributing fund, it covers the part of the full tax base that the distribution leaves open.

bloecke.formel:
Base return = Value on 1 January × Base interest rate × 0.7
Advance lump sum = Base return − Distributions for the year
Tax base = Distributions + Advance lump sum
bloecke.erklaerung: The advance lump sum is never less than zero and never greater than the annual gain (price increase plus distributions). For equity funds, the 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) under Section 20 InvStG is applied to the tax base first, then the saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag) and finally the tax rate of 26.375%.
variablen: upper limit of the advance lump sum, Section 18(1) InvStG
bloecke.beispiel: With a portfolio value of €50,000 on 1 January 2026, the base return is €1,120. Without a distribution, this is the full advance lump sum. With a distribution of €900, an advance lump sum of €220 remains; in both cases, the tax base is €1,120.

bloecke.titel: Tax base in 2026 with a portfolio value of €50,000
bloecke.unter: Both bars are the same height, because for the distributing fund the advance lump sum tops up the part that the distribution leaves open. Illustrative calculation under Section 18 InvStG, base interest rate 3.20%, distribution 1.8%.

bloecke.md:
In a normal rising year, the same amount of tax is therefore due on both variants. The tax base is €1,120; after the 30% [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption]], €784 is taxable, and with the [[Saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag)|saver's allowance]] used up, this results in €206.78 of flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) including solidarity surcharge. The widespread claim that accumulating funds have a tax advantage dates from the years in which the base interest rate was zero. It does not apply to the normal case in 2026.

## Years with a different tax burden

In three situations, the two variants are taxed differently, and in all three the accumulating fund has the advantage. First, the advance lump sum may not exceed the annual gain. In a year with a small gain, it is correspondingly small. The distribution, by contrast, is money received and is taxable in full regardless of the fund's performance. Second, the advance lump sum is zero in a loss year, while the distribution is still paid and taxed. Third, when the base interest rate is low, the base return is below the distribution. The accumulating fund is then taxed only on the base return, the distributing fund on the full distribution. With a distribution of 1.8%, this was the case in every year from 2018 to 2025. During the zero interest rate period in 2021 and 2022, there was no advance lump sum at all, because the base interest rate was negative, and holders of distributing funds paid tax on their distributions as usual.

bloecke.titel: Tax in euros for a €50,000 portfolio in four types of year
zeilen: Base interest rate zero or negative

bloecke.md: Illustrative calculation with a distribution of €900, a 30% partial exemption, a tax rate of 26.375% and the allowance used up. The differences do not mean a permanently higher tax burden; the distributing fund merely pays the tax earlier. If a taxed distribution is reinvested, new units with their own acquisition costs are created, and correspondingly less tax is due on the later sale. The accumulating fund keeps the money in the market for longer, and that is its entire advantage.

bloecke.titel: Base return and distribution yield, 2018 to 2026
bloecke.unter: Only in 2026 is the base return above the distribution of 1.8% assumed for a broad world ETF; in 2023 and 2025 it was just below. Until 2025, the distribution determined the tax base for the distributing fund; in 2026 it is the base return, and the two variants converge as a result.

bloecke.titel: Advance lump sum for distributing funds
bloecke.md: The statement “with a distributing fund, I have no advance lump sum” is only true if the distribution reaches the base return, which in 2026 means 2.24% of the portfolio value at the start of the year. A broadly diversified world ETF distributes less. Even investors who deliberately bought the distributing class must therefore expect a debit in January 2027.

## Saver's allowance and advance lump sum

For years, the most important practical argument for distributing funds was the saver's allowance, currently €1,000 (Section 20(9) EStG, Income Tax Act; €2,000 for joint assessment; until 2022 it was €801 and €1,602). It was only used reliably with distributions; otherwise it lapsed. That was true as long as the base return was close to zero. With a base interest rate of 3.20%, the taxable part of the advance lump sum is 1.568% of the portfolio value (base interest rate times 0.7, then times 0.7 for the partial exemption). Even a pure accumulating fund therefore uses up the allowance from a portfolio value of around €63,800 at the start of the year.

bloecke.titel: Portfolio value at the start of the year from which the advance lump sum alone uses up the allowance

bloecke.md:
Own calculation from the published base interest rates and today's allowances for an equity fund with a 30% partial exemption, without other capital income. The table also shows how strongly the argument depends on the level of interest rates. In 2019, a single person with the allowance of €801 at the time would have needed around €314,000 in the portfolio; in 2021, it was not possible at all. For investors who are currently building up a portfolio of considerably less than €60,000 and want to be sure of using the allowance, a distributing class remains the more convenient route. The difference, however, is only a few tens of euros a year.

## The effort of reinvestment

In the accumulation phase, the distribution mainly means extra work. The money sits in the settlement account and is not invested there. With the allowance used up, €733.84 of a €900 distribution is available for reinvestment. This requires an order, often with a fee and frequently with a delay. Many brokers offer automatic reinvestment. Where it is not available, a small cash balance remains uninvested permanently.

bloecke.unter: Thanks to the partial exemption, €270 remains tax-free and €630 is taxed. Illustrative calculation with the saver's allowance used up, excluding church tax.

bloecke.md:
## Distribution and partial sale in the withdrawal phase

A common piece of advice is to rely on distributing funds in retirement. The money then flows in without any action on your part, nobody has to sell units in a crash, and the number of units in the portfolio is preserved. This is psychologically convincing and organisationally simple. In tax terms, however, it is the more expensive route, because a distribution is 100% income, while in a partial sale only the gain portion is taxed.

A portfolio is worth €400,000 and the cost basis is €200,000, so the gain portion is 50%. The investor needs €10,000, and the allowance has been used up.

- With a withdrawal via the distribution, the full €10,000 is income. After the 30% partial exemption, €7,000 remains taxable, and the tax is €1,846.25.
- With a partial sale, €10,000 of proceeds contains €5,000 of gain. After the partial exemption, €3,500 is taxable, and the tax is €923.13. In addition, the advance lump sums previously recognised for the units sold reduce the capital gain (Section 19(1) InvStG).

Here the partial sale costs half as much. The longer the portfolio runs, the higher the gain portion and the smaller the gap. With a gain portion of 70%, the partial sale costs €1,292.38, while the distribution still costs €1,846.25. Investors who spend a distribution in full anyway lose nothing extra as a result. If, on the other hand, only part of it is needed and the rest is reinvested, money has been taxed that could have stayed in the portfolio.

A switch from the accumulating to the distributing class of the same fund looks like an internal transfer. For the custodian bank, however, these are two different ISINs, so it books a sale and a new purchase. The tax on the entire accumulated gain becomes due at once, and the tax deferral built up over several decades is used up. Investors who want regular distributions in retirement are therefore better off buying the second class in addition and leaving the existing holding untouched.

1. Decide on the distribution policy before the first purchase. It appears in the fund name as “Acc” or “Dist” and in the prospectus.
2. Issue the exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag) before the turn of the year, or split it across several banks. The advance lump sum is booked in the first days of January. An order issued later in the year applies to the whole calendar year, and the bank then refunds the tax already withheld retrospectively.
3. In December, check whether there is enough balance in the settlement account. If there is not, a debit balance can arise on which interest is charged.
4. Do not leave distributions lying idle. If they are collected and invested once a year, the loss is small. If, on the other hand, the money flows into day-to-day spending, less is saved than the savings plan suggests.

For funds without partial exemption, the distribution and the advance lump sum are taxed in full. This affects bond funds, money market funds and other funds that receive a partial exemption of 0% under Section 20 InvStG. All tax amounts in this lesson rise by just over 42% for them. The portfolio values from which the advance lump sum uses up the allowance, on the other hand, fall by 30%, in 2026 to around €44,600 for single people.

With a securities account abroad, brokers that do not deduct German tax remit neither flat-rate withholding tax nor tax on the advance lump sum. You have to declare both yourself on the capital income annex (Anlage KAP) and the investment fund income annex (Anlage KAP-INV), which means calculating the advance lump sum yourself. The only point in favour of accumulating funds here is that one payment item is eliminated; the effort remains.

With high distribution rates, for example for dividend or high-yield ETFs, the distribution is regularly above the base return. The advance lump sum then disappears entirely, and the tax base is permanently higher than for a comparable accumulating fund. Only in this case does the distribution policy noticeably increase the ongoing tax burden.

mitnehmen: Distribution and accumulation change nothing about wealth and differ only in the timing of taxation and the effort of reinvestment.
As long as the base return is above the distribution yield (in 2026, 2.24% against the 1.8% assumed here), the annual tax base is identical for both variants.

The accumulating fund is never worse off, but it has an advantage only in lean years, in loss years and in years in which the base return is below the distribution (2018 to 2025 with a distribution of 1.8%).
Since 2026, the advance lump sum fills the saver's allowance from a portfolio value of around €63,800, which means the old argument for distributing funds has lost much of its weight.
In the withdrawal phase, a partial sale is more tax-efficient than a distribution, because only the gain portion is taxed, whereas switching share class realises the entire gain at once.

begriffe.text: Reinvestment of income within the fund assets instead of a payout. The unit price rises accordingly, and no money flows to the investor.
Variant of the same fund with its own ISIN but an identical portfolio. The classes differ in distribution policy, currency hedging or minimum investment; the securities held are the same.

Notional minimum return of a fund under Section 18 InvStG, calculated as the value on the first valuation day of the year times the base interest rate times 0.7. After deducting distributions, the remainder is the advance lump sum.
Specification in the prospectus of whether a fund distributes or accumulates. In the fund name, it can be recognised by the suffix “Dist” or “Acc” respectively.
